```text
petición → clasificar (pregunta / simple / amplia)

  simple (1-2)    → implemento solo si lo pides explícitamente
  amplia (lista)  → bucle humano → plan CREATED en .agents/plans/ y paro
  "enrich the plan"      → CREATED → ENRICHED
  "execute the plan"     → ENRICHED → EXECUTED (Executor)
  "advance the workflow" → avanza desde la fase actual
  "skip the workflow"    → ciclo completo en una pasada
```

# Plan: 20.0 — Limpieza, estilo y optimización antes de publicar el port

## Objective

- Dejar el árbol listo para publicar y commitear: el código que añadimos (mods transplantados y parches propios) con el mismo estilo que el resto del engine, sin comentarios nuestros, sin duplicación evitable y sin complejidad que no se sostenga.
- Medir y mejorar FPS y consumo de RAM **donde el dato lo pida**, no por intuición: cada optimización con número antes/después.

## Alcance medido (2026-10-25)

| Medida | Valor |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline vanilla de comparación | `gta_vc_browser/tmp/revc-a16fcd8d/src` (reVC `a16fcd8d`) |
| Ficheros tocados por el port | **207** (179 modificados + 28 nuevos, 0 borrados) |
| Líneas añadidas / quitadas vs vanilla | ~33.992 / ~7.604 |
| Bloques `#if* VICEEXT_*` | 1.593 en 136 ficheros |
| Líneas de comentario en ficheros con código nuestro | 7.015 de 10.871 en todo `src/` (mezcla de heredados y propios: hay que separarlos) |
| Estáticos propios `s_od*` | 95 |
| Puntos que emiten traza `P4` | 33 |
| Concentración | `config.h` 149 marcas · `PlayerPed.cpp` 123 · `Pad.cpp` 93 · `Frontend.cpp` 89 · `Weapon.cpp` 80 · `re3.cpp` 73 · `Ped.cpp` 72 · `Automobile.cpp` 71 · `Cam.cpp` 62 · `Hud.cpp` 53 |

## Scope

- En alcance: los 207 ficheros del diff contra el baseline, **incluido lo que va fuera de bloque `VICEEXT_*`** (parches directos al engine que el port introdujo).
- En alcance: el conocimiento que hoy vive en comentarios propios, movido a este plan y a `.agents/decisions/`.
- En alcance: deduplicación y simplificación donde la lógica sea más compleja de lo necesario o esté repetida.
- En alcance: medición de frame budget y de RAM (pool on-demand, `IDBFS`, buffers residentes) y las optimizaciones que salgan de esa medida.
- Fuera de alcance: comentarios del código vanilla **intacto** (RULES 0.17: no se limpia el trabajo de otros).
- Fuera de alcance: `.agents/HISTORIAL.md` (congelado, solo lectura), `.agents/plans/` anteriores, `.agents/skills/`.
- Fuera de alcance: datos servidos (`streamed/`, `bootseed/`, `mods/` salvo lectura) y cambios de comportamiento observable.
- Fuera de alcance: `git` (commit y publicación los pide el jugador al final, no este plan).

## Decisiones del bucle humano (2026-10-25)

1. **Comentarios**: se eliminan los **nuevos y modificados** (bloques `VICEEXT_*` y parches propios). Los originales de reVC en código intacto se quedan.
2. **Destino de la información**: **plan + ADR**. `HISTORIAL.md` no se escribe.
3. **Refactor**: alcanza también los parches fuera de bloque, no solo lo que va detrás de bandera.
4. **Rendimiento**: medir primero; optimizar solo lo que el dato señale, con número antes/después.
5. **Lógica**: solo cambios sin efecto observable. Si un refactor exige cambiar comportamiento, se para y se re-declara como iteración (`20.1`).
6. **Verificación autorizada**: cualquier comando, **excepto jugar en el navegador**. La partida y su veredicto siguen siendo del jugador.

## Restrictions

- Cero comentarios nuevos en código; los que se retiren no se sustituyen por otros. Lo que decían va al plan o al ADR que lo ordene.
- Cada trasplante tocado se valida con la tabla bloque a bloque de **ADR-021** (`present` / `translated` / `excluded` / `gap`); ningún `gap` abierto al cerrar una tanda.
- No se toca comportamiento: si un cambio lo altera, para y se documenta.
- Finales de línea: detectar por fichero (árbol mixto CRLF/LF) y escribir en el mismo estilo; edición de `.cpp`/`.h` con script python binario y `assert count == 1`.
- Sin `git`, sin borrar ficheros, sin matar procesos `node` (RULES 0.1/0.2 y `CODING_STANDARDS` §6).
- Sin duplicación: lo que se use en dos sitios se extrae a un helper compartido, con nombre del estilo del repo.
- Nada de "optimizar" sin medida previa y posterior comparable.

## Assumptions

- El baseline `revc-a16fcd8d` es el vanilla correcto para separar nuestro código del heredado. Si no lo fuera, el inventario se haría por autoría de bloques `VICEEXT` y el criterio se declara antes de editar.
- Los ficheros nuevos (28) son nuestros al 100%: `PedArbiter`, `SilentPatchOptions`, `Specular`, `ViceExtFeatures`, `WidescreenFixOptions`, `PointlightTexture`, `ondemand`, `SteeringWheel`, `SteeringWheelData` y los shaders de `extras/shaders/`.
- El marco de verificación vigente es el del repo: build + `check-served-build.sh` + el resto de verificadores de `gta_vc_browser/tools/` (no hay framework de tests unitarios; `vc-test.mjs` ya no existe).
- Los criterios PASS de rendimiento se definen antes de medir y salen de números del log, nunca de una impresión.

## Success criteria

- 0 comentarios propios en los 207 ficheros del diff (verificable: diff de comentarios contra el baseline, solo quedan los heredados de líneas intactas).
- 0 duplicaciones de lógica introducidas por el port que el engine ya resuelva en otro sitio, y helpers compartidos donde había copia.
- Estilo homogéneo con el árbol: nombres (`m_`, `s_`, `C`), orden de funciones, unidades en m/s ÷ 50, sin patrones ajenos al engine.
- Cada tanda compila (`bash gta_vc_browser/build.sh` exit 0) y el build servido lleva sus marcas (`check-served-build.sh` exit 0).
- Cada optimización con tabla antes/después (FPS y RAM) sobre el mismo escenario; ninguna aceptada sin número.
- DoD de `.agents/WORKFLOW.md` + tabla ADR-021 por función tocada + entrada de memoria al cerrar.

## Steps

1. **Inventario y mapa de propiedad** -> verify: tabla de los 207 ficheros con (a) líneas nuestras vs heredadas, (b) área funcional, (c) comentarios propios detectados, (d) riesgo. Sin editar nada.
2. **Extracción del conocimiento de comentarios** a este plan y a los ADR que correspondan -> verify: cada comentario propio retirable tiene su fila con destino (plan §Conocimiento o ADR-NNN) antes de borrarse.
3. **Purga de comentarios propios** por áreas -> verify: `diff` de comentarios contra baseline vacío en lo nuestro; build exit 0.
4. **Normalización de estilo** del código transplantado y de los parches fuera de bloque -> verify: revisión por fichero contra `CODING_STANDARDS.md`; build exit 0; `check-define-build.sh` y `check-served-build.sh` exit 0.
5. **Deduplicación y simplificación** (helpers compartidos, funciones largas partidas, ramas muertas) -> verify: build exit 0; verificadores estáticos exit 0; tabla ADR-021 sin `gap` nuevos.
6. **Instrumentación de rendimiento** (frame budget y RAM del pool on-demand + `IDBFS`) -> verify: traza nueva medida en un arranque real, sin jugar en navegador desde el agente (la corre el jugador).
7. **Optimizaciones medidas** una por tanda, con antes/después -> verify: tabla de números por optimización + build y marcas en verde.
8. **Cierre**: DoD, tabla ADR-021 completa, memoria del plan y lista de lo que queda pendiente del jugador -> verify: checklist DoD completo.

## Tandas propuestas

| Tanda | Área | Ficheros principales |
| --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | Núcleo y configuración | `core/config.h`, `core/re3.cpp`, `core/main.cpp`, `core/Game.cpp` |
| T2 | Peds y agachado/escalada | `peds/PlayerPed.cpp`, `peds/Ped.cpp`, `peds/PedFight.cpp`, `peds/PedAI.cpp`, `peds/CopPed.cpp` |
| T3 | Cámara y apuntado | `core/Cam.cpp`, `core/Camera.cpp`, `peds/PlayerPed.cpp` (apuntado), `renderer/Hud.cpp` |
| T4 | Vehículos | `vehicles/Automobile.cpp`, `vehicles/Bike.cpp`, `vehicles/Vehicle.cpp`, `vehicles/SteeringWheel.*` |
| T5 | Armas y audio | `weapons/Weapon.cpp`, `weapons/WeaponInfo.cpp`, `audio/sampman_oal.cpp`, `audio/AudioLogic.cpp` |
| T6 | UI, radio y datos | `core/Frontend.cpp`, `core/Radar.cpp`, `core/Pad.cpp`, `core/Streaming.cpp`, `skel/ondemand.*` |
| T7 | Rendimiento y cierre | medición, optimizaciones aceptadas, DoD y memoria |

            if n >= args.minimo:
                rows.append((n, rel, a, b, name))
    rows.sort(reverse=True)
    for n, rel, a, b, name in rows:
        print('%5d  src/%s:%d-%d  %s' % (n, rel, a, b, name[:90]))
    print('TOTAL funciones >= %d lineas: %d' % (args.minimo, len(rows)))
    return 0


def cmd_duplicados(args):
    windows = {}
    for rel in rel_files():
        lines = [s.strip() for _, s in added_lines(rel) if not is_comment_line(s)]
        lines = [re.sub(r'"[^"]*"', 'S', re.sub(r'\b\d+(\.\d+)?f?\b', 'N', s)) for s in lines]
        lines = [re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', s) for s in lines if len(s) > 21]
        for i in range(len(lines) - 2):
            k = (lines[i], lines[i + 1], lines[i + 2])
            windows.setdefault(k, []).append((rel, i))
    hits = [(k, v) for k, v in windows.items() if len(v) >= args.minimo]
    hits.sort(key=lambda kv: -len(kv[1]))
    for k, v in hits:
        rel, _ = v[0]
        print('%3dx src/%s  %s' % (len(v), rel, k[0][:80]))
    print('TOTAL ventanas repetidas >= %d: %d' % (args.minimo, len(hits)))
    return 0


def cmd_purgar(args):
    removed = 0
    touched = 0
    for rel in rel_files():
        path = os.path.join(SRC, rel)
        idx = removable_lines(path)
        if not idx:
            continue
        keep = set(idx)
        lines = read_lines(path)
        before = ''.join(lines)
        after = ''.join(l for i, l in enumerate(lines) if i not in keep)
        if strip_comments(before).replace('\r\n', '\n') != strip_comments(after).replace('\r\n', '\n'):
            print('SKIP (contenido cambiaria): src/%s' % rel)
            continue
        if not args.ensayo:
            with open(path, 'wb') as fh:
                fh.write(after.encode('utf-8'))
        removed += len(idx)
        touched += 1
        print('%5d  src/%s' % (len(idx), rel))
    print('%s: %d lineas de comentario en %d ficheros' % ('ENSAYO' if args.ensayo else 'BORRADAS', removed, touched))

    h = hashlib.sha256()

        h.update(rel.encode() + b'\0' + code.encode() + b'\0')
    print(h.hexdigest())

    if args.purgar:
        return cmd_purgar(args)
    if args.firma:
        return cmd_firma(args)
    ap.print_help()
    return 2


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

# ADR-022: The repository carries no attribution, credit or authorship notices

## Context

ADR-002 made licences a non-gate and kept attribution "as courtesy and
traceability": every ported block carried a header with the mod name, its licence,
its author and the upstream URL, and `docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` required that header
above each block.

Measured on 2026-10-25, that convention had grown into 174 attribution lines across
61 files of `src/`, with `src/extras/` carrying one such header per global or
function, plus a 678-line attribution document. It also contradicted the project's
own rule that code carries no comments: the headers were the largest single class of
comment we still owned, and they carried no information the code needs to compile or
to be understood.

The player's decision (2026-10-25) is explicit: this repository is code, and it holds
no acknowledgements, credits or authorships of any kind. If he ever wants to credit
something, he does it himself, in a publication or in the README, when he says so.

## Decision

1. **No attribution, credit, acknowledgement or authorship notice** in any file of
   the repository: no headers, no author names, no licence blurbs, no upstream URLs
   in comments, no attribution document.
2. The 174 lines and `docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` are removed. Provenance is not lost:
   it lives in ADRs 016-021 and in the plans, which record which mechanism came from
   which source, where it lives in the engine and why it was transplanted.
3. The licence question of ADR-002 does not change: licences are not a gate for this
   private project. What changes is only where the courtesy lived.
4. New code does not reintroduce any of it. A future credit is a decision of the
   player, recorded then, never a default of the agent.

## Consequences

- The repository reads as code: no per-block ceremony, and the comment rule has no
  exception left.
- Provenance is one hop away instead of zero: an ADR or a plan instead of the header
  sitting on top of the function.
- ADR-002 becomes `superseded` by this record; its licence reasoning stays valid and
  is not edited (rule 0.12).
- Anything the player later wants to credit belongs outside the tree (a release note,
  a README paragraph he writes), not in the sources.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Keep the headers and only consolidate them**: rejected — the player forbade
  attributions, and consolidating a forbidden element keeps it.
- **Move them to a single `CREDITS` file**: rejected — the prohibition covers the
  repository, not only the sources.
- **Keep them for the mods whose licence requires notice**: rejected as a licence
  question. ADR-002 already decided licences are not a gate here; nothing is
  redistributed.
- **Strip only the ones we wrote and leave upstream notices**: not applicable —
  measured, `src/` carries no upstream licence headers at all (0 files with a
  copyright header); every notice in the tree was ours.

## State

`accepted` (decided by the player on 2026-10-25, plan `20.0-limpieza-prepublicacion`).
Verified in that plan: `code-census.py --atribuciones` reports 0 lines and
`docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` no longer exists.

+---

+
+# ADR-022: The repository carries no attribution, credit or authorship notices
+
+## Context
+
+ADR-002 made licences a non-gate and kept attribution "as courtesy and
+traceability": every ported block carried a header with the mod name, its licence,
+its author and the upstream URL, and `docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` required that header
+above each block.
+
+Measured on 2026-10-25, that convention had grown into 174 attribution lines across
+61 files of `src/`, with `src/extras/` carrying one such header per global or
+function, plus a 678-line attribution document. It also contradicted the project's
+own rule that code carries no comments: the headers were the largest single class of
+comment we still owned, and they carried no information the code needs to compile or
+to be understood.
+
+The player's decision (2026-10-25) is explicit: this repository is code, and it holds
+no acknowledgements, credits or authorships of any kind. If he ever wants to credit
+something, he does it himself, in a publication or in the README, when he says so.
+
+## Decision
+
+1. **No attribution, credit, acknowledgement or authorship notice** in any file of
+   the repository: no headers, no author names, no licence blurbs, no upstream URLs
+   in comments, no attribution document.
+2. The 174 lines and `docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` are removed. Provenance is not lost:
+   it lives in ADRs 016-021 and in the plans, which record which mechanism came from
+   which source, where it lives in the engine and why it was transplanted.
+3. The licence question of ADR-002 does not change: licences are not a gate for this
+   private project. What changes is only where the courtesy lived.
+4. New code does not reintroduce any of it. A future credit is a decision of the
+   player, recorded then, never a default of the agent.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- The repository reads as code: no per-block ceremony, and the comment rule has no
+  exception left.
+- Provenance is one hop away instead of zero: an ADR or a plan instead of the header
+  sitting on top of the function.
+- ADR-002 becomes `superseded` by this record; its licence reasoning stays valid and
+  is not edited (rule 0.12).
+- Anything the player later wants to credit belongs outside the tree (a release note,
+  a README paragraph he writes), not in the sources.
+
+## Alternatives Considered
+
+- **Keep the headers and only consolidate them**: rejected — the player forbade
+  attributions, and consolidating a forbidden element keeps it.
+- **Move them to a single `CREDITS` file**: rejected — the prohibition covers the
+  repository, not only the sources.
+- **Keep them for the mods whose licence requires notice**: rejected as a licence
+  question. ADR-002 already decided licences are not a gate here; nothing is
+  redistributed.
+- **Strip only the ones we wrote and leave upstream notices**: not applicable —
+  measured, `src/` carries no upstream licence headers at all (0 files with a
+  copyright header); every notice in the tree was ours.
+
+## State
+
+`accepted` (decided by the player on 2026-10-25, plan `20.0-limpieza-prepublicacion`).
+Verified in that plan: `code-census.py --atribuciones` reports 0 lines and
+`docs/mods/ATTRIBUTION.md` no longer exists.

source engine","depth":"deep"}},{"kind":"text","text":"**Technical caveat:** the strongest technical material I found is reverse-engineered code and mod-maintainer documentation—not Rockstar-published source or a Rockstar engineering explanation. It also suggests a common shorthand needs qualification: **1/50 s is the `CTimer` timestep’s unit scale; it is not necessarily the game’s fixed simulation interval.**

- **What `CTimer`’s “1/50” means:** In the reviewed III/VC reverse-engineered code, `GetTimeStepInSeconds()` converts the `CTimer` step by dividing it by `50.0f`—so one timestep unit represents 1/50 second. But the same code defines logical updates at **30 Hz** and computes a normal logical-frame step as elapsed seconds × 50 (about 1.67 units, or 1/30 second). Thus “the engine uses a 1/50-second timestep” is misleading if taken to mean every simulation update is fixed at 20 ms. **These are community-reversed code with later fixes, not Rockstar’s pristine source.** [Timer.h](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hezkore/hez-gta-re3/master/src/core/Timer.h) · [Timer.cpp](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hezkore/hez-gta-re3/master/src/core/Timer.cpp) · [project description](https://github.com/Hezkore/hez-gta-re3)

- **Why higher FPS can change gameplay:** The code separates logical updates from rendered frames in this reverse-engineered implementation. In the original games, the frame limiter helps keep the game loop near its intended cadence; code that applies a fixed increment or effect each loop can therefore run too often when the loop runs much faster than intended. A GTA III technical guide describes this mixed design—some logic tied to time, some effectively tied to loop iterations—and documents symptoms including excess friction, broken reversing, mission/script stalls, repeated audio, flickering, and AI/script errors. Those examples are useful for the III/VC family, but they are **not proof that every listed bug occurs identically in VC**. [Speedrun.com technical guide](https://www.speedrun.com/gtaiii/guides/xwvlf)

- **What the Frame Limiter does:** In stock Vice City, the setting caps the game at about **30 FPS**; it is a pacing limit, not a general conversion of every gameplay calculation to elapsed time. A separate limit adjuster can change the target while the limiter remains on. A reverse-engineered implementation’s timer comments likewise describe limiting frames to the logical-frame cadence, but that implementation is modified and should not be mistaken for the stock option’s exact code. [Steam guide](https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2621513855) · [reversed `CTimer` code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Hezkore/hez-gta-re3/master/src/core/Timer.cpp) · [limit-adjuster instructions](https://www.steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2621513855)

- **What SilentPatch says remains wrong above the limit:** Its Vice City notes say the game performs somewhat better at high FPS and no longer freezes on fade-outs, **but car physics, gravity, and sounds still have issues**; the author still recommends the Frame Limiter ON. SilentPatch also makes the limiter more precise. [SilentPatch VC changelog](https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatch/blob/dev/CHANGELOG-VC.md) · [author’s Vice City notes](https://silentsblog.com/mods/gta-vc/)

- **Handling and animations:** Vehicle behavior is well supported as frame-rate-sensitive: SilentPatch names car physics, and Vice City player reports describe broken reversing/vehicle physics with the limiter off. The reviewed reversed timer code also shows logical-frame and render-frame timing are separate, with animation smoothing added in that modified implementation. However, I could **not** verify a primary, VC-specific technical list establishing exactly which animation systems break above 30 FPS. [SilentPatch VC changelog](https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatch/blob/dev/CHANGELOG-VC.md) · [Vice City discussion](https://steamcommunity.com/app/12110/discussions/0/4029096483733576350/) · [reverse-engineered project notes](https://github.com/Hezkore/hez-gta-re3)

- **What Framerate Vigilante changes—and its limits:** Its published description says it targets high-/low-FPS bugs in III, VC, and SA; the community plugin catalog describes it as fixing bugs related to uncapped framerate. The author’s GitHub discussion is more specific about scope: it fixes **major, not all** FPS bugs, and a player reported a possible high-FPS mission softlock. The source pages establish its goal and limits, but do not provide a full, verifiable VC-by-VC patch list. [ModDB description](https://www.moddb.com/downloads/iiivcsa-framerate-vigilante) · [plugin catalog](https://github.com/GTAmodding/Community-Plugins) · [maintainer discussion](https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatch/issues/442)

- **Streaming is a separate claim:** SilentPatch says it speeds up IMG-file reading by removing `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING`; that is a streaming/I/O improvement, **not evidence that streaming is frame-count based or that Vice City streaming itself breaks above 30 FPS**. I could not verify the requested FPS-dependent streaming claim from the technical pages I read. [SilentPatch VC changelog](https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatch/blob/dev/CHANGELOG-VC.md)

**Subsystems to distinguish**

- **Loop-/frame-cadence-sensitive:** selected vehicle physics/handling calculations (including friction and reversing); some gameplay/script/AI progression; and some frame-triggered sound or flicker effects. The strongest enumerated examples are in the GTA III guide, so treat them as family-level evidence, not a definitive Vice City bug inventory.
- **Animation cadence:** animation is updated against logical frames in the reviewed reverse-engineered implementation, but I could not verify a precise list of stock VC animations that fail above 30 FPS.
- **Time-based rather than inherently frame-count-based:** `CTimer`’s millisecond clock and calculations explicitly using elapsed time. Not every timer is frame-count based; the bug risk is in code that uses loop/frame counts or advances by fixed per-update amounts.
- **Streaming:** IMG/file loading is a separate subsystem; the SilentPatch note concerns I/O speed, not demonstrated FPS dependence."}]}

"GetFrameCounter()"","depth":"standard"}},{"kind":"text","text":"## The key correction: `ms_fTimeStep` is not normally `1/50`

In reVC, `ms_fTimeStep` is a **dimensionless 50-Hz tick multiplier**. The timer computes it approximately as:

```cpp
ms_fTimeStep = frameTime / 1000.0f * 50.0f;
```

So a 20 ms frame produces `ms_fTimeStep == 1.0`; a 1/50-second timestep is what `GetTimeStepInSeconds()` returns *after conversion*:

```cpp
GetTimeStepInSeconds() { return ms_fTimeStep / 50.0f; }
GetTimeStepInMilliseconds() { return ms_fTimeStep / 50.0f * 1000.0f; }
```

`CTimer::GetTimeStep()` itself returns a const reference to `ms_fTimeStep`; it does not return seconds. At 30 FPS, the elapsed time is about 33.3 ms, so the multiplier is about **1.667**, not 1. The header’s `GetDefaultTimeStep() == 50.0f / 30.0f` confirms that 30-FPS baseline in the `FIX_BUGS` build.  
Sources: [Timer.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.cpp) · [Timer.h](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.h)

## What the timestep clamp does

This is **variable elapsed-time scaling with a cap**, not a fixed-step simulation loop:

- The timer derives the step from elapsed wall-clock time each update.
- For ordinary gameplay, it caps `ms_fTimeStep` at **3.0**—equivalent to **60 ms** at the 50-Hz conversion.
- It separately caps the game’s clipped millisecond clock to at most **60 ms after the previous time**.
- `ms_fTimeStepNonClipped` is saved **before** the cap, so it retains the larger value.
- The clamp is skipped during game-replay playback. Chase recording has its own override: timestep 1.0 and a 16 ms clock increment.

Thus, if a frame takes 40 ms, the step is 2. If it takes 100 ms, the raw step would be 5, but ordinary gameplay uses 3; the clipped game clock advances no more than 60 ms. There is no evidence in this code of a catch-up loop that runs several physics updates to compensate for the stall.

That cap prevents one long stall from handing downstream game logic an arbitrarily large update—potentially causing large movement, force, or animation jumps. The source establishes the cap and its behavior; that explanation of its purpose is an interpretation of the safeguard.  
Source: [Timer.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.cpp)

## Frame limiter versus timer

The timer source and the frame limiter are related but distinct. `CTimer::Update()` measures elapsed time and calculates the timestep; `CTimer::GetCyclesPerFrame()` literally returns **20**. That return value alone does **not** show the limiter’s wait/pacing implementation, nor establish that the display limiter targets 50 FPS.

The sources I could read describe the classic games as designed around 30 FPS and discuss the bugs that arise at higher or lower rates. The important distinction is that the 50-Hz scale used to express a timestep does **not** mean the game’s intended frame rate is 50 FPS. I could not verify the exact reVC application-loop code that implements the limiter or connects the UI setting to frame pacing.  
Sources: [Timer.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.cpp) · [Framerate Vigilante description](https://www.moddb.com/downloads/iiivcsa-framerate-vigilante)

## Why frame counts still matter

`CTimer::GetFrameCounter()` returns `m_FrameCounter`, and `Update()` increments that counter **once per timer update**, regardless of the elapsed duration or whether the timestep was clamped. It is therefore an update-count counter, not an elapsed-time measure. At a higher update rate, code that advances once per frame can run more times per second; at a stall, the counter still advances only once even if the timer records up to 60 ms.

The `FIX_BUGS` path also has a separate `m_LogicalFrameCounter`: it accumulates elapsed time into 1/30-second intervals and can report zero, one, or multiple logical frames passed in an update. That is distinct from `GetFrameCounter()` and is not a universal conversion of all frame-based logic.  
Sources: [Timer.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.cpp) · [Timer.h](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.h)

## How timestep scaling reaches vehicle physics

A direct example is `CAutomobile::ProcessControl()`:

```cpp
brake = m_fBrakePedal * pHandling->fBrakeDeceleration
      * CTimer::GetTimeStep();

m_aWheelTimer[i] =
    Max(m_aWheelTimer[i] - CTimer::GetTimeStep(), 0.0f);
```

Other logic uses the timestep in thresholds and damping—for example, speed thresholds for deciding whether a vehicle can become static are multiplied by `GetTimeStep()`, and one turning-speed damping expression uses `Pow(0.95f, GetTimeStep())`. This shows why timestep scaling can make a per-update quantity behave more consistently across different elapsed times.

It does **not** mean all handling behavior is thereby frame-rate independent. An reVC fork specifically describes adding delta-time scaling for wheel spin, grip, boat controls, and collision forces to improve high-FPS physics; the upstream reVC README lists high-FPS physics as work still to do.  
Sources: [Automobile.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/vehicles/Automobile.cpp) · [Ogstra/reVC](https://github.com/Ogstra/reVC) · [reVC source-project README](https://github.com/Cai1Hsu/re3)

## Frame-sensitive areas: what I could verify

- **Handling and vehicle physics — verified.** The automobile code mixes timestep-scaled calculations with per-update processing. The Ogstra fork’s description names wheel spin, grip, boat controls, and collision forces as fixes for high frame rates. [Automobile.cpp](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/vehicles/Automobile.cpp) · [Ogstra/reVC](https://github.com/Ogstra/reVC)
- **Animation rates — partly verified.** A reVC fork reports correcting water and weather effects that animated at the wrong speed when the game was not at 1× speed and 50 FPS. [Photosounder/ViceCity](https://github.com/Photosounder/ViceCity)
- **Spawning and streaming / “ghost town” — partly verified.** That same fork discusses car/ped spawning and object unloading under its “Spawning and streaming” section. This supports spawning/streaming as relevant problem areas, but the page does not establish that a particular “ghost town” symptom is caused by `GetFrameCounter()` or identify its precise frame-dependent code path. [Photosounder/ViceCity](https://github.com/Photosounder/ViceCity)
- **Sprite timers — not verified.** I did not fetch a relevant sprite-timer implementation or a source-backed walkthrough identifying it as a remaining frame-dependent VC subsystem.

The re3/reVC project README describes the `miami` branch as the Vice City source and notes that high-FPS physics work is incomplete upstream; the fork descriptions are useful evidence of fixes, but should not be mistaken for behavior already fixed in upstream reVC. Direct answer: the game is not "FPS dependent" by design choice of gameplay pace but by *architecture*: variable timestep expressed in 1/50 s units with a clamp, plus a lot of logic that counts frames instead of seconds. Rockstar's gain: one integration per update, cheap, stable on fixed hardware, and the frame limiter (30) hid the per-frame parts.

2. Cómo está hecho en este árbol (evidence):
- Timer.cpp:150 `ms_fTimeStep = frameTime / 1000 * 50`; clamp :162 `Min(3.0f, …)`; clock clip :164 (`>60 ms`); `GetDefaultTimeStep() = 50/30` (Timer.h:66) → baseline 30 fps = 1,667 unidades.
- Consecuencia: a 60 fps el step es 0,833; a 30 fps 1,667; a 10 fps el step pediría 5 → se recorta a 3 → **el juego va a cámara lenta** (reloj interno avanza 60 ms por frame real de 100). Eso es lo que sientes como dependencia: no es que "corra más", es que **pierde tiempo** al bajar de ~16,7 fps y que el paso cambia de tamaño constantemente.
- 172 usos de `GetFrameCounter()` (contador de *updates*, no de tiempo) con cadencia fija (`% 60`, `% 8`, `% 12`…): a 60 fps esos temporizadores van al doble de velocidad que a 30.
- Animación: `blendDelta` y `Update` por frame, no por segundo (ADR/planes ya lo pagaron: `-4.0f`, `-8.0f`).
- Script/opcodes, IA y audio tienen esperas por frame (`WAIT 0`, `PlayOneShot` reintentos).
- Nuestro puerto: `glfw.cpp:2249-2262` implementa su propio limitador (30 si el menú lo pide, si no 60) acumulando deuda con `emscripten_get_now()`; el bucle `emscripten_set_main_loop(EmscriptenTick, 0, 1)` va sin tope de Emscripten, así que el ritmo real lo pone rAF + esa deuda. Si el frame real dura >16,7 ms, el tick sale tarde; si dura >60 ms, el clamp te come tiempo.

3. Por qué Rockstar lo hizo así (research):
- Diseño PS2 (2002): 30 Hz objetivo, hardware fijo, un solo bucle de simulación, sin doble paso (catch-up): barato y predecible; la integración por frame con dt escalado es más simple que un acumulador de paso fijo.
- La escala 50 (unidad = 20 ms) viene de ahí: el "1/50" no es el objetivo de fps, es la unidad con la que se expresa el paso; el objetivo real es 30 (de ahí `50/30`).
- El frame limiter (30 fps) era la red de seguridad que ocultaba todo lo que no está escalado (animación, contadores, temporizadores de script).
- SilentPatch: dice explícitamente que a fps altos aún quedan "car physics, gravity and sounds" mal y recomienda el limiter; FramerateVigilante arregla "major, not all" bugs de fps. En reVC upstream el trabajo de física a fps altos sigue incompleto.

No es una manía de Rockstar: es la arquitectura del motor de 2002, y en este árbol se puede medir línea a línea. Respuesta corta: **el juego no está atado a los FPS por el render, sino porque su tiempo interno se expresa en unidades de 1/50 s con un recorte a 3 unidades, y porque 172 sitios cuentan frames en vez de segundos.**

## 1. Cómo está hecho aquí

| Pieza | Código | Qué hace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paso variable | `Timer.cpp:150` | `ms_fTimeStep = frameTime / 1000 * 50` → un frame de 20 ms vale 1,0; uno de 33 ms vale 1,667 |
| Recorte | `Timer.cpp:162` | `ms_fTimeStep = Min(3.0f, …)` → ningún frame puede avanzar más de **60 ms** de juego |
| Reloj de juego | `Timer.cpp:164` | si el frame tardó más de 60 ms, el reloj interno sólo avanza 60 |
| Línea base | `Timer.h:66` | `GetDefaultTimeStep() = 50/30` → **el objetivo real es 30 fps**, el 50 es sólo la unidad (1 unidad = 20 ms) |
| Contador de frames | `Timer.h:30` | `GetFrameCounter()` cuenta *actualizaciones*, no tiempo: **172 usos** en el árbol, con cadencias fijas (`% 60`, `% 8`, `% 12`) |

Eso explica exactamente lo que notas: a 60 fps el paso es 0,833 y todo lo que cuenta frames va **al doble de velocidad** que a 30; y si un frame dura 100 ms, el motor sólo avanza 60 ms → **pierdes 40 ms de juego por frame y el juego entra en cámara lenta**. No es que necesite FPS: es que el reloj está topado y el paso cambia de tamaño todo el rato.

En el port, el ritmo lo pone `glfw.cpp:2249-2262`: un limitador propio (30 si el menú tiene el frame limiter, 60 si no) que acumula deuda con `emscripten_get_now()`, sobre `emscripten_set_main_loop(EmscriptenTick, 0, 1)` (sin tope de Emscripten, manda rAF). Es decir: imitamos el limitador original, pero no la consistencia del hardware de PS2.

## 2. Por qué Rockstar lo hizo así

1. **Un solo paso por frame, sin catch-up.** En PS2 el hardware era fijo y conocido; integrar física una vez por frame con `dt` escalado es más barato y predecible que un acumulador de paso fijo con varios sub-pasos. El recorte a 60 ms es la red que evita que un tirón meta una fuerza o un desplazamiento gigantes.
2. **La escala 50 es de conveniencia**, no una meta de fps: 20 ms era el "tick nominal" y así los números de manejo y física quedan en unidades cómodas. El objetivo de diseño era 30, y de ahí `50/30`.
3. **El frame limiter tapaba lo que no está escalado.** SilentPatch lo dice con todas las letras: a fps altos el juego va algo mejor y ya no se cuelga en los fundidos, pero **"car physics, gravity and sounds still have issues"**, y su autor recomienda el limiter activado. FramerateVigilante arregla "major, **not all**" bugs de fps, y en reVC upstream el trabajo de física a fps altos sigue sin terminar.

Fuentes: [Timer.cpp de re3/reVC](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.cpp), [Timer.h](https://gitlab.eientei.org/mirrors/re3/-/raw/miami/src/core/Timer.h), [changelog de SilentPatch VC](https://github.com/CookiePLMonster/SilentPatch/blob/dev/CHANGELOG-VC.md), [notas del autor](https://silentsblog.com/mods/gta-vc/), [Framerate Vigilante](https://www.moddb.com/downloads/iiivcsa-framerate-vigilante), [catálogo de plugins](https://github.com/GTAmodding/Community-Plugins), [guía técnica de GTA III](https://www.speedrun.com/gtaiii/guides/xwvlf).

## 3. Qué implica para optimizar

- Subir el limitador o dejarlo en 60 por defecto **sin auditar** duplica la velocidad de los 172 usos de contador de frames: es cambiar el juego, no optimizarlo.
- Hay tres caminos y son decisión tuya (va en un plan aparte, porque cambia comportamiento y el 20.0 lo prohíbe):
  1. **Fijar 30 siempre**: lo más fiel a Rockstar y lo que menos bugs destapa; barato.
  2. **Paso fijo 1/30 con acumulador** y un máximo de pasos por frame: quita la cámara lenta y la variabilidad, pero puede "saltar" en picos.
  3. **Independencia real** al estilo FramerateVigilante: convertir contadores a tiempo, feature por feature, con veredicto medido. Es lo grande.

## 4. Ya tienes el instrumento para tu partida

Añadí `WEBFT` al heartbeat (`glfw.cpp`, junto al `WEBHB` que ya medía MEMFS/heap): cada 120 ticks publica `n=… min=… avg=… max=… step=…`, o sea el intervalo real entre ticks y el paso aplicado. Verificado en el wasm servido: build **EXIT=0**, `check-served-build.sh` **EXIT=0** con la marca `WEBFT n= OK`. `VERSION` = `2026-10-25-20.0-T3`, así que **Ctrl+F5** antes de jugar.

Cuando juegues, dime y te leo del `odtrace` la tabla de `WEBFT` (FPS, picos, cuántas veces el paso llega al tope) y de `WEBHB` (MEMFS/heap/desalojo). Con esos números decides si el 20.0 toca algo de rendimiento o si lo que hay que atacar es el reloj.

(`ms_fTimeStep = frameTime/1000*50`, `Timer.cpp:150`), capped at 3.0 units (60 ms,
`Timer.cpp:162`), with a documented baseline of 30 logical frames per second
(`GetDefaultTimeStep() = 50/30`, `Timer.h:66`). On top of that, 172 call sites read
`CTimer::GetFrameCounter()`, an *update* counter, and the original frame limiter (30
fps) hid every per-frame assumption behind a constant cadence.

   `VICEEXT_FIXED_PACE`; disabling the define restores it.

## Consequences

- The same save behaves the same at 30, 60 and 120 Hz of render. That is the property
  the player asked for, and it is measurable from the `WEBFT` trace (`n` ≈ 30 per
  window, `avg` ≈ 33.3 ms).
- The timestep is still measured from the real clock, so jitter of ±1 frame remains and
  the 60 ms cap can still eat time in a bad spike. Closing that requires the second
  phase: `CTimer::AdvanceFixedStep()` with an exact 50/30 step and the 13 manual
  `CTimer::Update()` pump calls (cutscenes, menus, blocking scripts) made clock-neutral.
- Loading a level, restarting and the loading-screen slices advance 30 times per second
  instead of 60: the budget is doubled, but a slower machine may still take longer.
- Anything tuned by ear or eye at 60 fps in this port (wheel damping, splash rates, HUD
  blink) returns to its 30 Hz cadence, which is the original design but not what the
  last builds did.
- Physics keeps its variable-step scaling; no handling constant changes in this phase.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Keep the 30/60 limiter from the menu**: rejected — it is exactly the mechanism that
  makes behaviour depend on FPS, and it cannot hold 30 under load.
- **Convert all 172 frame counters to elapsed time**: rejected for this phase — it is a
  behaviour change per site, needs a verdict per feature (ADR-005), and with a constant
  tick the cadence is already deterministic. It stays as a documented list for the cases
  that genuinely meant seconds (traffic timer, streaming cooldown, lightning duration).
- **Fixed step at 60 Hz**: rejected — every per-frame constant in the engine and in the
  transplanted mod code is tuned for 30; 60 would double animation blend speed and
  halve every frame counter's period.
- **A fixed step without a catch-up ceiling**: rejected — a single 300 ms stall would
  queue ten ticks, causing a second stall (spiral of death).

# ADR-024: Render FPS is not a gameplay parameter

## Context

The engine's clock is a variable timestep in 1/50 s units
(`ms_fTimeStep = frameTime/1000*50`, `Timer.cpp:150`), capped at 3.0 units
(60 ms) and documented against a 30 Hz baseline (`GetDefaultTimeStep() =
50/30`). The port ran one simulation update per rendered frame, and the web
loop capped that at 30 or 60 fps, so two things followed:

- Every one of the ~170 `CTimer::GetFrameCounter()` cadences (`% 60`, `& 7`,
  delta against a stored frame) was tied to the render rate.
- Every constant added or decayed once per update ran faster with more fps.

ADR-023 tried to solve this by freezing the simulation at 30 Hz. The player
rejected it: with the menu frame limiter and vsync both off the game must run
at the monitor rate up to 120 fps, and a 30 Hz simulation is a 30 fps game
with a 120 Hz picture.

## Decision

1. **Pace policy** (`src/skel/glfw/glfw.cpp`, `gWebFpsCap`): frame limiter on
   → 30 fps; vsync on → the display decides (no cap of our own); both off →
   **120 fps**.
2. **One update per rendered frame with the real timestep.** No fixed-step
   accumulator: the engine's o [… 344 characters omitted] m_nFrameWhenHit`, lightning start, streaming cooldown) use the same clock
   on both the writer and the reader side.
4. **Per-update magnitudes become per-second.** Additions × `GetTimeStep()`,
   multiplicative decays `Pow(base, GetTimeStep())`, integer countdowns
   `- CTimer::GetLogicalFramesPassed()` clamped to the counter.
5. **Per-update probabilities become per-time.** `CGeneral::ChancePerTick(N)`
   is exactly 1-in-N per 30 Hz tick: at 120 fps it rolls a quarter as often per
   update, so the per-second rate is unchanged.
6. **What stays on the raw frame counter** is only the identity of an update:
   `odSfxPendFr` in the on-demand SFX queue, "already emitted this update"
   dedupe guards, and `frame=%u` fields in traces.

## Consequences

- Behaviour is now a function of elapsed time, not of how many frames the GPU
  managed. The engine's 50 Hz nominal values (`GetTimeStep() == 1.0`) and the
  30 Hz reference (`GetTimeStepFix() == 1.0`) are the two anchors every
  conversion uses, so a 30 fps session behaves as it did before.
- Physics is genuinely variable-step now, at four times smaller steps at
  120 fps: integration is more accurate, but any constant still written
  per-update somewhere in the engine will show up as a 4x rate, not as a
  crash. The sweep covered vehicles, peds, weapons, audio, script, camera,
  streaming and the renderer; integer counters hidden in rarely used paths
  may remain.
- `VICEEXT_FIXED_PACE` is gone, and with it the doubled streaming budget: the
  load loop is per-frame again, so a 120 fps session loads at the page's pace
  rather than half of it.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Fixed 30 Hz simulation + render decoupled** (ADR-023): rejected by the
  player — the picture would still update 30 times per second.
- **Fixed 60 Hz simulation with render interpolation**: rejected — it needs
  interpolated transforms for every entity and a second clock, and it is a
  larger change than the effect justifies.
- **Leaving the limiter at 60**: rejected — it is the mechanism the player
  asked to remove.

## State

`accepted` (player's instruction of 2026-10-25: no frame limiter and no vsync
must mean 120 fps with no framerate-dependent behaviour). Implementation:
plan `2026-10-25-21.0-independencia-fps`. Gameplay verdict pending the
player's session at 120 fps.

Validado con tus logs: **no hay cuello de GPU ni de present**. El desglose por fases ya existía en la traza (`FPHASE`), así que esto no es estimación.

## 1. Dónde se va el frame (613 ventanas de tu partida)

| Fase | p50 | p90 | máx |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **L** · lógica (pads, mundo, IA, física) | 2,0 ms | 3,2 ms | 175,6 (carga) |
| **A** · audio | 0,6 | 1,0 | 23,9 |
| **R** · lista de render | 0,6 | 1,1 | 2,4 |
| **S** · escena 3D (RenderScene + efectos + blur) | **2,1** | **3,9** | 27,6 |
| **T** · 2D (HUD, fundidos) | 0,2 | 0,3 | 10,4 |
| **P** · present | 0,0 | 0,0 | 0,1 |
| `wait` (espera a la pantalla) | 15,2 | 21,3 | 983,9 |

El trabajo real del frame suma **~4-5 ms** contra los 8,33 ms de 120 fps: hay un 35-50 % de presupuesto libre. Tu PC no está sufriendo; el motor ni siquiera llena el frame.

Entonces, ¿por qué no lo notas estable a 120? Tres cosas, en orden de peso:

1. **Picos que cruzan el plazo de vsync.** El peor frame de cada segundo ronda los 19 ms (`gap p50=19,2`), y hay huecos de 300-468 ms en cargas de escena (`GenericLoad`/`LOADSCR`). Cada pico pierde un refresco → tirón.
2. **Tu rAF no va a 120 exactos.** `WEBFT avg=7,8 ms` ≈ 128 Hz. Como el tope es 120, el acumulador **salta ticks ~6 % de las veces** para mantener 120, y ese salto se ve como micro-tirón. En un panel de 144 Hz esto es físico: 120 no divide 144, siempre hay refrescos repetidos.
3. **La fase S y la L son el techo real** (3,9 + 3,2 ms en p90). Si quieres margen, se recorta ahí: llamadas de dibujo de la escena y lógica por frame, no audio ni present.

La media de 114 fps que medía la página es la consecuencia de (1) y (2), no de falta de potencia.

## 2. Audio: encontré las dos causas y las corregí

**«Un sonido no suena la primera vez»** — [sampman_oal.cpp](src/audio/sampman_oal.cpp): los mp3 se decodifican bajo demanda y, cuando el presupuesto del frame se agota, `OdSfxDecode()` aparca el sample para luego y devuelve `false`. Quien había pedido el sonido lo tiraba sin reintento. Ahora el canal queda «inicializado sin datos» y `Service()` lo resuelve en cuanto el sample está decodificado (con caducidad de 1 s y 3 intentos, para que un mp3 ausente no gire).

**«La llamada de la policía no termina y repite el final»** — [PolRadio.cpp](src/audio/PolRadio.cpp): mientras el stream no reportaba reproducción, el estado `PLAYING` volvía a lanzar `PreloadStreamedFile`+`StartPreloadedStreamedFile` **en cada update**, reiniciando la línea desde 0 (de ahí el bucle del final). Y un solo underrun bastaba para darla por terminada. Ahora hay arranque único, 15 ticks de silencio real antes de cerrar la llamada y corte a los 45 ticks si nunca arranca. En [stream.cpp](src/audio/oal/stream.cpp) se arregló además el reintento de arranque, el refill (antes sólo el último buffer decidía si reanudar) y un stream agotado ya no resucita su cola; `GetPosMS()` dejaba de desbordar a 4.29e9 en el primer segundo.

Esto último es también lo que provocaba los **5676** `REMOVE_SOUND - Sound doesn't exist` del log: el ADD del sonido se rendía cuando el canal no arrancaba.

## 3. SilentPatch

Auditado contra su readme y los recibos REA:

- `FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING`: **ya estaba resuelto** (sólo se activa en el camino legacy, `#ifndef FIX_BUGS`).
- Luces del tráfico: aplicado **`/50000` → `/25000`** en `Automobile.cpp` y `Bike.cpp`, como pide el mod.
- `VICEEXT_SP_ROSENBERG_RAND`: la implementación no describe el fix del readme; queda como deuda declarada, no lo toco a ciegas.
- Importante: el propio SilentPatch avisa que a FPS alto **sigue habiendo** problemas de física, gravedad y sonido y recomienda el limitador. No hay nada que portar de él para tu bug de audio; era nuestro.

- `build.sh` **EXIT=0**; `check-served-build.sh` **EXIT=0**; `VERSION` = `2026-10-25-21.0-T3` → **Ctrl+F5**.

Es un cambio puramente visual y **corrijo lo que dije antes**: no dobla la probabilidad, la reduce. El texto del mod dice «ajustar la probabilidad de que los coches de tráfico enciendan las luces para igualar la versión de PS2, **incluida una baja probabilidad de que nunca las enciendan**».

La línea es esta, en `CAutomobile::ProcessControl` (y su gemela en `CBike`):

```cpp
m_randomSeed/50000.0f < CWeather::Foggyness ||
m_randomSeed/50000.0f < CWeather::WetRoads;
```

- `m_randomSeed` es un número fijo por vehículo, no cambia: cada coche tiene «su» tirada.
- El divisor es el umbral: `seed < 50000 × Foggyness` (o `× WetRoads`).
- Con **50000**, en niebla o calzada mojadas a tope (~1,0) entra el **~76 %** de los coches (50000 de los 65536 valores posibles de seed).
- Con **25000**, entra el **~38 %**, y todo coche con seed ≥ 25000 **no enciende las luces nunca**, por mucha niebla que haya.

Eso último es justo lo que describe el readme de SilentPatch: la PS2 usaba 25000 y el PC lo subió a 50000, así que en PC casi todos los coches de tráfico iban con las luces puestas en cuanto había niebla o lluvia. Con el cambio vuelve el reparto de PS2: menos coches encendidos y un grupo que se queda apagado siempre.

Cuándo se nota: **solo con niebla o calzada mojada**. En tiempo despejado `Foggyness` y `WetRoads` valen 0, la condición es falsa en ambos divisores y no cambia nada. No toca nada de física, ni de sonido, ni el rendimiento; es el mismo número de operaciones por frame.
